note: Plain-English definitions shown when someone taps a dotted-underlined term. 'match' lists the exact phrases to underline (case-sensitive, longest first). Keep definitions neutral and short.

terms.definition: A 1973 Supreme Court decision that recognized a constitutional right to abortion, generally until viability. The Court overturned it in 2022.

match: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization
terms.definition: The 2022 Supreme Court decision that overturned Roe v. Wade, letting states and Congress set abortion law.
The point in pregnancy, around 24 weeks, when a fetus could survive outside the womb.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 lowered income-tax rates, nearly doubled the standard deduction and cut the corporate rate from 35% to 21%. Many individual cuts were due to expire after 2025 until the 2025 budget law made them permanent.

The 2025 budget law, called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It made most 2017 tax cuts permanent, added new deductions such as for tips and overtime, and reduced projected spending on Medicaid and food aid.
A 2022 law that created tax credits for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles, and let Medicare negotiate some drug prices. The 2025 budget law ended many of its energy credits early.
People brought to the U.S. without legal status as children. About half a million are protected from deportation under DACA, a 2012 program, but have no path to citizenship.
Legal protection for people who fear persecution in their home country. People usually apply after reaching the U.S. or its border.
A legal process that would let people living in the U.S. without legal status eventually become citizens, usually after background checks, fees and a waiting period.
2020 agreements, brokered by the U.S., in which the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan established relations with Israel.
An independent Palestinian state alongside Israel, long the stated goal of U.S. diplomacy.
Territory between Israel and Jordan, held by Israel since 1967. About 3 million Palestinians and roughly half a million Israeli settlers live there.
Replacing a country's government, by force or by pressure.
A strategy of heavy economic sanctions meant to force a government to change course.
Penalties such as trade bans and frozen assets aimed at a country, company or person.
A military alliance of the U.S., Canada and 30 European countries. Members pledge to defend each other if attacked.
Taxes on imported goods. The importing business pays them first, and often passes some of the cost on to buyers.
Rules that bar selling certain technology, such as advanced computer chips, to other countries.
The 2010 health law, also called Obamacare. It created subsidized insurance marketplaces, let states expand Medicaid, and bars insurers from refusing people with pre-existing conditions.
Proposals to replace private health insurance with one government plan that covers everyone.
A government-run health plan people could choose instead of a private plan.
Health coverage for people with low incomes, run by states with federal money.
Fixed federal payments to states, instead of funding that grows with the number of people enrolled.
Rules that people must work, study or volunteer a set number of hours a month to keep a benefit.
Background checks on every gun sale, including private sales. Today federal law requires them only for sales by licensed dealers.
Laws that let a court temporarily remove guns from someone judged a danger to themselves or others.
A ban on certain semi-automatic rifles with military-style features. A federal ban was in place from 1994 to 2004.
Carrying a hidden handgun in public, usually with a state permit. National reciprocity would make one state's permit valid in every state.
Removing as much greenhouse gas from the air as is released, so the overall total added is zero.
Realistic fake video, audio or images made with AI.
Large buildings full of computers that run AI and online services. They use a lot of electricity and water.
Public money families can use toward private-school tuition or other education costs.
Publicly funded schools that run independently of the local school district.
Money a person charged with a crime pays to be released before trial. It is returned if they come to court.
Each state's military reserve force. Governors command it, but the president can take control of it.
A Senate rule that lets 41 of 100 senators block most bills, so most laws need 60 votes.
Proposals to give Supreme Court justices a fixed term, often 18 years, instead of serving for life.
Conduct rules for justices. The Supreme Court adopted a code in 2023, but nobody outside the Court enforces it.
Requiring voters to show identification before casting a ballot.
Requiring documents such as a passport or birth certificate to register to vote. Only citizens may vote in federal elections already; this would change how that is checked.
